passages.title: Reading Passage 1 · The Thread That Built an Empire
passages.note: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1.
paras: For more than two thousand years, silk was among the most valuable goods in the world. It was light enough to carry over long distances, beautiful enough to be desired by the rich, and, for most of its history, mysterious to everyone except the Chinese. The story of how this fabric was made, guarded and eventually shared is also the story of trade, politics and, at times, deliberate deception.

Silk is produced by the larva of a moth, Bombyx mori, commonly known as the silkworm. Over a period of about a month, the larva eats enormous quantities of mulberry leaves and grows to around ten thousand times its original weight. It then spins a cocoon from a single continuous thread, which may be as long as nine hundred metres. To obtain the thread intact, producers must stop the insect before it breaks out of the cocoon as an adult moth. Traditionally this was done by placing the cocoons in hot water or steam, which also softens the natural gum that holds the thread together, so that it can be unwound.

According to Chinese legend, silk was discovered around 2700 BC by Leizu, the wife of the Yellow Emperor, when a cocoon fell into her cup of tea and began to unravel. The story cannot be confirmed, but archaeology shows that silk production in China is extremely old. Fragments of silk fabric found in a tomb in Henan province have been dated to around 3600 BC, and carved images of silkworms appear on objects that are older still.

For many centuries, the Chinese state treated the methods of silk production as a secret of national importance. Revealing them to foreigners, or attempting to take silkworm eggs out of the country, could be punished by death. This monopoly made silk enormously profitable. The network of land and sea routes that connected China with Central Asia, India, the Middle East and Europe later became known as the Silk Road, although the name was invented only in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen, and the routes carried many other goods, including spices, glass, horses and paper, as well as ideas and religions.

In Rome, silk became so fashionable that some writers complained about it. The philosopher Seneca criticised silk clothing for being so thin that it hid nothing, while others worried that the fashion was draining the empire of gold, since silk had to be paid for in precious metal. The Romans themselves had only a vague idea of where silk came from; some believed it grew on trees.

The secret could not be kept for ever. Silk production spread to Korea by around 200 BC, probably with migrants from China, and later to Japan. In the West, the most famous episode took place in the sixth century AD. According to the historian Procopius, two monks arrived at the court of the Byzantine Emperor Justinian, offering to bring back silkworm eggs from Central Asia. They are said to have hidden the eggs inside hollow walking sticks. Whether or not the details are accurate, the Byzantine Empire did establish its own silk industry soon afterwards, and for several centuries the city of Constantinople controlled the supply of silk to Europe.

By the late Middle Ages, Italian cities such as Lucca, Venice and Florence had become major centres of silk weaving, and in the sixteenth century the French king supported the industry in Lyon, which became the capital of European silk. Attempts to produce silk in England were less successful. In the early seventeenth century, King James I ordered thousands of mulberry trees to be planted in London, but the trees chosen were mostly of the black variety, while silkworms strongly prefer the leaves of the white mulberry. The project produced very little silk.

In the nineteenth century, the European silk industry was almost destroyed by a disease called pébrine, which killed silkworms in vast numbers. The French government asked the chemist Louis Pasteur to investigate. Pasteur, who had no previous knowledge of silkworms, discovered that the disease was caused by a tiny parasite and could be passed from the female moth to her eggs. He developed a method of examining each female under a microscope and destroying the eggs of any infected moth. His approach saved the industry, although by then many producers had already turned to imported Japanese eggs.

Today, China and India together produce the great majority of the world's raw silk. Scientists, meanwhile, are interested in silk for reasons that have little to do with fashion. Silk is strong, flexible and compatible with the human body, and researchers are developing silk-based materials for uses that include surgical stitches, coatings that keep food fresh and even components for electronic devices. After five thousand years, the thread spun by a small caterpillar may still have a future.

passages.title: Reading Passage 2 · Waiting in Line
passages.note: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2.
paras: A  Most people in developed countries spend a surprising amount of their lives waiting in line: at supermarkets, airports, banks and, increasingly, on the telephone or online. Estimates vary, but one frequently quoted figure suggests that the average person in a large city spends several days a year queuing. Not surprisingly, businesses have become very interested in the experience of waiting, and a field of research has developed around a simple question: why do some waits feel longer than others?

B  One of the earliest contributions came not from psychology but from mathematics. In 1909, a Danish engineer, Agner Krarup Erlang, was asked to work out how many telephone operators were needed to deal with calls to the Copenhagen telephone exchange. His equations, which predict how long a queue will become depending on how quickly people arrive and how quickly they are served, are still the basis of queuing theory. They allow managers to calculate, for example, how many checkouts a supermarket must open to keep waiting times below a target.

C  However, mathematics alone cannot explain why customers become frustrated. In a well-known article published in 1985, the researcher David Maister argued that the way people feel about a wait matters as much as its actual length. Among his principles was the idea that unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time. A famous, though possibly exaggerated, example concerns an airport in Houston where passengers complained about long waits for their luggage. Instead of employing more baggage handlers, the airport moved the arrival gates further from the baggage hall, so that passengers spent more time walking and less time standing still. The complaints are said to have almost disappeared.

D  Uncertainty also makes waiting more stressful. When people do not know how long they will wait, they tend to imagine the worst. This is why many theme parks display estimated waiting times at the entrance to each ride, and why some deliberately overestimate them: visitors who expect to wait forty minutes but are served after thirty feel pleased, while those who expect twenty and wait thirty feel cheated, even though the actual wait is identical. Similarly, studies of telephone helplines have found that callers are more likely to hang up if they hear music alone than if they are regularly told their position in the queue.

E  Perhaps the strongest emotions are caused by a sense of unfairness. People are often more upset by someone pushing in ahead of them than by the length of the wait itself. For this reason, many banks and post offices replaced several separate lines with a single 'serpentine' queue that feeds into all the counters. Mathematically, a single line is usually more efficient, but its main advantage may be psychological: no one has the frustrating experience of watching a neighbouring line move faster than their own.

F  Cultural differences also play a part. In Britain, queuing is often described as a national habit, and breaking the rules of a queue is regarded as a serious social offence. In other countries, crowds at a counter may be organised less formally, yet people may still have clear expectations about who should be served next. Researchers who have filmed queues in different cities have found that even where there is no visible line, people frequently keep track of the order in which others arrived, and will object if this order is not respected.

G  Technology is now changing the nature of waiting. Many restaurants and clinics give customers a 'virtual' place in a queue and send a text message when it is their turn, allowing them to wait elsewhere. Some theme parks sell tickets that allow visitors to skip the line altogether, although this has proved controversial, as it can create resentment among those who cannot afford to pay. For businesses, the lesson of a century of research appears clear: reducing the length of a wait is valuable, but managing how the wait feels may be just as important, and often much cheaper.

passages.title: Reading Passage 3 · Can Machines Be Creative?
passages.note: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3.
paras: In 2018, a portrait of a blurred, dark-coated gentleman was sold at an auction in New York for more than four hundred thousand dollars, many times its estimated price. The painting had not been made by a human artist but by a computer program trained on thousands of historical portraits. Since then, software that can produce images, music and text in response to a short written instruction has become available to millions of people. These developments have reopened an old question: can a machine be genuinely creative, or is it simply imitating creativity?

Part of the difficulty lies in defining creativity itself. Many psychologists accept a definition that has two parts: a creative product must be new, and it must also be valuable or useful in some way. A random sequence of notes is new but not usually valuable; a perfect copy of a famous song is valuable but not new. By this standard, it seems difficult to deny that some machine-made works are creative, since they are original arrangements that some people clearly value. Critics reply that this definition focuses only on the product and ignores the process. In their view, creativity requires intention, an understanding of what one is trying to achieve, and machines have no intentions of their own.

The British researcher Margaret Boden has proposed a useful distinction between three kinds of creativity. Combinational creativity involves putting familiar ideas together in unfamiliar ways, as when a poet compares love to a journey. Exploratory creativity involves working within an established set of rules, such as a musical style, and discovering what is possible within it. Transformational creativity, the rarest kind, changes the rules themselves, as happened when artists abandoned perspective in the early twentieth century. Boden has argued that computers are already good at the first two kinds, but that transformational creativity remains far more difficult for them, partly because a system must recognise which rules are worth breaking.

Supporters of creative machines point out that human artists also learn by absorbing the work of others. No composer invents music from nothing; each has listened to thousands of pieces, and their style is shaped by what they have heard. If a human is not accused of mere imitation for learning in this way, why should a machine be? Opponents respond that the comparison is misleading. A human artist does not simply recombine examples but brings personal experience, emotion and a particular view of the world to their work. A program that has never felt grief, they argue, cannot write about grief in any meaningful sense, however convincing the result may appear.

Interestingly, studies of how people respond to machine-made art suggest that our judgements are influenced by what we believe about its origins. In several experiments, participants rated the same paintings or poems less favourably when they were told that a computer had produced them than when they were told that a human was responsible. This suggests that part of the value we place on art depends on the sense of communication between one mind and another. It also raises the possibility that, as people become used to machine-made works, this bias may weaken.

There are also practical and legal questions. In many countries, copyright law protects only works that have a human author, which means that images produced entirely by software may not be protected at all. Artists, meanwhile, have complained that their work has been used without permission to train these programs, and several legal cases on this issue are still in progress. Some musicians and illustrators fear for their livelihoods, particularly in areas such as advertising, where speed and cost often matter more than originality.

Not all artists see the technology as a threat, however. Some use it as a tool, much as photographers use cameras or musicians use synthesisers, generating dozens of rough ideas quickly and then selecting, editing and combining the most promising ones. For these artists, the creative act lies less in producing the first draft than in recognising what is worth keeping. In this sense, the arrival of creative software may change our idea of the artist from a maker of objects to something closer to an editor or director.

Ultimately, whether machines can be creative may depend less on the machines than on how we choose to use the word. If creativity is defined purely by results, then the answer is already yes. If it requires consciousness and intention, then the answer is no, at least for now. What seems certain is that the debate will force us to think more carefully about what we value in human creativity, and why.
